scope: 27 already existing, mock-eligible, short AQA Physics and Chemistry original core cards, 12 Physics and 15 Chemistry (AS and selected already-taught A2)
purpose: Target user's observed weaknesses: slope forces, graph gradients and areas, optics/particles, uncertainty, energy and Hess signs, Kp, rate laws, mass spectrometry, ester chemistry. Require full correct concepts and reject specific misconceptions.
limitations: Scope is 27 original short cards, not an exhaustive three-subject AQA specification audit.
A passing tested set cannot certify all possible unseen paraphrases; manual review remains available.
Retain the exact original front/back, mock flags, old card IDs and saved progress.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: For a slope at angle θ, what are the components of weight parallel and perpendicular to the slope?
rows.originalBack: Parallel = mg sin θ. Perpendicular = mg cos θ. If no other perpendicular force acts and there is no perpendicular acceleration, R = mg cos θ.
accept: Parallel weight component is mg sin θ; perpendicular is mg cos θ, so R=mg cos θ if there are no other normal forces.
Along the incline: mg sin theta; normal to incline: mg cos theta; the normal reaction equals mg cos theta in the stated simple case.
reject: Parallel = mg cos θ; perpendicular = mg sin θ.
Weight parallel to the slope is mg and the normal reaction is always zero.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Why does a filament lamp's resistance rise at high current?
rows.originalBack: The filament gets hotter, increasing lattice vibrations and electron collisions.
accept: The hotter filament vibrates more, increasing electron scattering and therefore resistance.
At higher current the filament temperature increases; greater lattice vibration raises resistance.
reject: Resistance falls as the hotter filament's ions vibrate less.
The rise in current cools the filament and reduces collisions.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Velocity rises uniformly from 4 to 12 m s⁻¹ in 5 s. Find displacement.
rows.originalBack: Area under v–t graph = ½(4+12)×5 = 40 m.
accept: 40 metres, using mean speed 8 m/s for five seconds.
Displacement = ((4+12)/2)×5 = 40 m.
reject: Displacement is 20 m.
Displacement = 12 × 5 = 60 m.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: For a Hookean force–extension graph (F vs ΔL), what do gradient and area give?
rows.originalBack: Gradient = spring stiffness k; area = work done / elastic strain energy (for elastic loading).
accept: Gradient is k, spring stiffness; area beneath the force-extension graph is elastic potential energy.
Slope gives the spring constant, while area under F against extension gives stored elastic strain energy.
reject: Gradient gives elastic energy and area gives spring stiffness.
Both gradient and area give force, not work or stiffness.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: For free fall from rest, what is g from a graph of v² (y) against s (x)?
rows.originalBack: v² = 2gs, so gradient = 2g and g = gradient ÷ 2.
accept: For v squared against s, gradient = 2g; divide the gradient by two for g.
g is half of the v²–distance slope because v² = 2gs.
reject: g is equal to the gradient of the v² against s graph.
g is twice the gradient of the v² against s graph.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: For a wire, how is Young modulus found from a force (y) vs extension (x) graph?
rows.originalBack: Gradient = F/ΔL; E = gradient × original length L ÷ cross-sectional area A.
accept: Young modulus E = (force-extension gradient × original wire length) / wire cross-sectional area.
From the F against ΔL slope, E = gradient × L/A.
reject: Young modulus equals force-extension gradient multiplied by cross-sectional area divided by length.
Young modulus E = gradient divided by the original length and by area.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is the photon energy when an excited electron falls to a lower level?
rows.originalBack: E = hf = E(high) − E(low), using the positive energy difference.
accept: Emitted photon energy hf is the higher electron level energy minus the lower one.
Energy released is ΔE = Eupper − Elower = hf, taken positive.
reject: Emitted energy equals E(lower) minus E(higher), giving a negative photon energy.
A photon emitted in a downward transition has zero energy.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Why can atoms absorb photons of only certain frequencies?
rows.originalBack: Only photons whose energy hf matches an allowed energy-level gap can be absorbed.
accept: Only photons with hf equal to an allowed separation between electron levels are absorbed.
Atomic energy levels are discrete, so the incoming photon must match an allowed energy difference.
reject: Atoms absorb all frequencies continuously regardless of energy levels.
Absorption occurs only when photon energy is smaller than every possible electron energy gap.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Velocity falls from +6 to −2 m s⁻¹ uniformly in 4.0 s. Find a and the time of reversal.
rows.originalBack: a = (−2−6)/4 = −2.0 m s⁻². v = 0 after 3.0 s; direction then reverses.
accept: Acceleration = −2.0 m/s²; zero velocity is reached after 3.0 s.
a = (−2−6)/4 = −2 m s⁻² and direction changes at t = 3 s.
reject: Acceleration is +2 m/s² and direction reverses after 3 s.
Acceleration is −2 m/s² and the object reverses direction at 1 s.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What powers of ten do micro (μ) and nano (n) mean?
rows.originalBack: micro = 10⁻⁶; nano = 10⁻⁹.
accept: micro is 10 to the power −6, nano is 10 to the power −9.
reject: micro is 10^-9 and nano is 10^-6.
μ means 10^-3 while n means 10^-6.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: For quantities multiplied, how do percentage uncertainties combine?
rows.originalBack: Add their percentage uncertainties.
accept: Add the fractional percentage uncertainties for multiplied measurements.
For multiplication, the combined percentage uncertainty is the sum of the input percentage uncertainties.
reject: Multiply the percentage uncertainties together.
Subtract the smaller percentage uncertainty from the larger one.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: How is uncertainty in a graph gradient estimated?
rows.originalBack: Compare the steepest and shallowest acceptable gradients.
accept: Use the maximum and minimum gradients from steepest and shallowest acceptable lines to estimate gradient uncertainty.
Compare the highest and lowest valid graph slopes around the best-fit line to assess the uncertainty.
reject: Only the best-fit gradient matters; acceptable extreme lines are irrelevant.
Take the steepest possible gradient as an exact value with zero uncertainty.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How do you find order from initial-rate experiments?
rows.originalBack: Compare two trials holding other concentrations constant; see how the rate responds.
accept: Compare initial-rate trials in which only one reactant concentration changes, then relate its rate factor to the concentration factor.
Hold the other concentrations fixed, alter A, and use the rate change to find A's order.
reject: Change every reactant concentration together and assign each the overall order.
Reaction orders can always be read directly from the balanced equation coefficients.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How do you find unknown total pressure P from Kp and mole fractions?
rows.originalBack: Replace each partial pressure p(A) by x(A)×P in Kp, simplify the powers of P, then solve.
accept: Use partial pressures p_i = mole fraction_i × total pressure P in Kp, then rearrange for P.
Substitute x_i P for each equilibrium partial pressure and solve the resulting Kp equation for total pressure.
reject: Replace partial pressure p_i with x_i/P before solving Kp.
Put the initial, rather than equilibrium, mole fractions into Kp without considering reaction progress.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How is transesterification different from hydrolysis?
rows.originalBack: Transesterification exchanges an ester group; hydrolysis breaks an ester bond.
accept: Transesterification swaps the alcohol-derived part of an ester; hydrolysis breaks the ester using water.
One ester is converted to another by reaction with alcohol in transesterification, whereas hydrolysis cleaves ester bonds with water.
reject: Transesterification specifically splits esters with water, whereas hydrolysis swaps the alcohol group without water.
Both processes only oxidise the ester and preserve its bond unchanged.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Should you use initial or equilibrium concentrations in Kc?
rows.originalBack: Equilibrium concentrations only. Find these from a mole-change table if necessary.
accept: Use equilibrium values for concentration in the Kc expression, not initial concentrations.
Only concentrations after equilibrium is reached belong in Kc; calculate them first if necessary.
reject: Use starting concentrations in Kc without allowing for the reaction.
Kc is calculated using concentrations before equilibrium is established.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How do you calculate reaction molar ΔH using solution q?
rows.originalBack: ΔH=−q_solution(kJ)/moles of reaction, with sign chosen correctly.
accept: Molar enthalpy change equals negative heat gained by the solution in kJ divided by moles of reaction.
ΔH = −q_solution/(1000 n) if solution heat q is in J and n is the equation's mole extent.
reject: ΔH = +q_solution/n for an exothermic reaction that warms the solution.
Molar ΔH is found by multiplying q in kJ by the number of reaction moles.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What happens to the measured magnitude of exothermic ΔH if heat escapes?
rows.originalBack: The temperature rise is too small; calculated ΔH is less negative.
accept: Heat escaping makes the measured temperature rise smaller and the calculated exothermic ΔH closer to zero.
The measured enthalpy change is less exothermic, meaning a less negative ΔH.
reject: Heat loss makes the temperature increase larger and the calculated ΔH more negative.
Heat loss leaves the experimental temperature rise and ΔH completely unaffected.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the molar enthalpy formula if q_solution is in joules?
rows.originalBack: ΔH = −q_solution/(1000 × n) in kJ mol⁻¹.
accept: ΔH in kJ/mol = −q in joules divided by (1000 × moles reacted).
ΔH = −q/(1000n) kJ mol^-1 when q is heat gained by the solution in J.
reject: ΔH = −1000q/n in kJ mol^-1 when q is joules.
ΔH = −q n/1000 instead of dividing by n.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: For ΔfH° values, which subtraction order gives reaction ΔH?
rows.originalBack: Sum of products − sum of reactants, including coefficients.
accept: For standard formation enthalpies use sum of coefficient-weighted products minus sum of coefficient-weighted reactants.
Reaction ΔH = ΣνΔfH(products) − ΣνΔfH(reactants).
reject: For formation enthalpies, calculate reactants minus products.
Ignore all stoichiometric coefficients when summing standard formation enthalpies.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: For ΔcH° values, which subtraction order gives reaction ΔH?
rows.originalBack: Sum of reactants − sum of products, including coefficients.
accept: With standard combustion enthalpies calculate coefficient-weighted reactants minus coefficient-weighted products.
ΔH reaction = ΣνΔcH(reactants) − ΣνΔcH(products).
reject: For combustion enthalpies take products minus reactants.
Combustion-cycle enthalpies must never be multiplied by equation coefficients.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the general bond-enthalpy estimate for reaction ΔH?
rows.originalBack: Sum of energies for bonds broken − sum of energies for bonds formed.
accept: Enthalpy estimate is total bond energy to break bonds minus total bond energy released on forming bonds.
ΔH = Σ(bond enthalpies broken) − Σ(bond enthalpies formed).
reject: ΔH = bond energies formed minus bond energies broken.
Add bond-breaking and bond-forming contributions as two positive terms.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why does equal kinetic energy not mean equal speed?
rows.originalBack: Since Eₖ=½mv², lighter ions have greater speed at equal Eₖ.
accept: At equal kinetic energy E = ½mv², lighter ions must move faster than heavier ions.
Velocity varies inversely with the square root of mass for equal KE, so smaller mass means larger speed.
reject: Equal kinetic energy always gives equal ion speed regardless of mass.
At the same kinetic energy, the heavier ion must travel faster.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why might the electrospray [M+H]⁺ peak differ from molecular mass?
rows.originalBack: It includes the mass of an added proton; m/z is about Mr+1 for 1+ ions.
accept: Electrospray protonation adds H+, so singly charged [M+H]+ has m/z approximately Mr + 1.
The observed [M+H]+ ion contains one extra proton, making its mass-to-charge ratio about one unit greater.
reject: The [M+H]+ peak must be one mass unit lower because a proton was removed.
Electrospray adds an electron with a mass of one dalton to give [M+H]+.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why rinse a pipette with the measured solution first?
rows.originalBack: To avoid diluting it with residual water.
accept: Rinse with the analyte solution to stop leftover rinse water diluting the solution measured by the pipette.
Pre-rinsing with the actual solution prevents residual distilled water lowering its concentration.
reject: Leave distilled water in the pipette so the measured solution is diluted.
Rinsing with an unrelated solution improves concentration accuracy.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What makes a substance electrophilic rather than nucleophilic?
rows.originalBack: Electrophiles accept electron pairs; nucleophiles donate electron pairs.
accept: An electrophile accepts a pair of electrons while a nucleophile donates a pair.
Electrophiles are electron-pair acceptors; nucleophiles are electron-pair donors.
reject: An electrophile donates electron pairs and a nucleophile accepts them.
Both nucleophiles and electrophiles are defined solely as electron-pair donors.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the stoichiometric number of fatty acid methyl esters per triglyceride?
rows.originalBack: Three methyl ester molecules correspond to one triglyceride.
accept: Each triglyceride yields three fatty acid methyl ester molecules in complete transesterification.
One triglyceride produces three FAME molecules because it has three fatty acid residues.
reject: One triglyceride gives only one methyl ester molecule.
One triglyceride gives only two fatty acid methyl esters.
